opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that language is already a highly compressed, human-designed abstraction. When we invented words, we did a huge amount of the hard work up front: we carved the world into discrete symbols, each carrying a lot of meaning. So when you train a model to predict the next token, you're operating in a space where the structure is already there, and the signal-to-noise ratio is extremely high. That's a big part of why language modeling has worked so well.

Continuous spatial signals, like images, video, and the physical world we move through, are a completely different kind of thing. There's no natural vocabulary. A pixel by itself means almost nothing. The information is massively redundant, high-dimensional, and full of details that don't matter for understanding, like exact textures, lighting noise, or tiny variations in a leaf. If you take the language-modeling recipe and apply it directly, tokenizing the image and predicting the next patch or pixel, you end up spending enormous capacity modeling low-level detail instead of learning the underlying structure: geometry, objects, physics, how things persist and interact in three-dimensional space over time.

There's also a deeper point. Language is fundamentally a one-dimensional sequence, and autoregression fits that shape very naturally. Space isn't sequential in that way. There's no canonical order for scanning a scene. Imposing a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order on the world is an artifact of borrowing the method, not something the world itself suggests.

And finally, a lot of what we call spatial intelligence isn't expressed in language at all. Think about how a cat jumps onto a table, or how you reach for a cup without looking. That understanding is grounded in perception and action, not in description. If our models only learn the world through the lens of text, or through methods designed for text, they inherit text's blind spots. They can talk about the world fluently without really having a model of it.

So I don't think language modeling is wrong. It's incredibly powerful. But I think we need representation-learning approaches that are native to continuous, spatial, embodied signals, ones that learn what to abstract away and what to keep, rather than assuming the world comes pre-tokenized the way language does.

r001.rationale: The response says spatial signals are highly redundant and explains that tokenizing images into patches or pixels spends capacity on low-level detail rather than underlying structure.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes token-by-token modeling of low-level detail but does not state that transformers must pay equal attention to every token or identify this as an inductive bias.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Well, I'd be a bit careful with the framing. I don't think language-modeling techniques "cannot" solve it — they've already gotten us surprisingly far. What I'd say is that they're not sufficient on their own, and the reason comes down to what the data actually is.

Language is already a compressed, discretized abstraction. Humans did the hard work over thousands of years of turning the world into tokens — words, syntax, concepts. So when you train a language model, you're learning the statistics of something that was designed to be symbolic and sequential. Next-token prediction fits that beautifully.

The physical world isn't like that. Vision, 3D space, motion — these are continuous, high-dimensional, and extremely redundant signals. There's no natural tokenizer. When we force an image or a video through a discrete codebook and then treat it like a sentence, we're throwing away a lot and also imposing a one-dimensional ordering on something that has no inherent order. Pixels in the top-left corner don't "come before" pixels in the bottom-right. So you end up spending a huge amount of capacity learning to undo the artifacts of your own representation.

The second issue is what the model is actually being asked to learn. In language, predicting the next word forces you to build a fairly rich world model, because the text was written by humans who already understood the world. In vision, if you just predict the next patch, the easiest solution is often to model low-level texture and color statistics. That's not the same as understanding that there's a cup on a table, that the cup has a back side you can't see, that if you push it, it'll fall. Spatial reasoning — object permanence, geometry, physical causality — these are things we learn from embodied interaction, not from reading, and current multimodal LLMs are quite weak at them even when they're very strong at describing a scene.

So my view is we need visual representations that are learned from the signal itself, self-supervised, that capture geometry and dynamics, and then connect those to language. Language becomes an interface for reasoning and communication, not the substrate for perception. A lot of our recent work — looking at how well these systems actually "see" versus how well they talk about what they see — points to that gap. The models are great at the talking part. The seeing part still needs its own foundation.

r001.rationale: The response calls visual and spatial signals highly redundant and discusses tokenizing images or video, but does not state that serializing a global world state into tokens produces that redundancy.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify equal attention to every token as an inductive bias of transformers.

astra-6.text:
I would be careful with the word “cannot.” I don’t think there’s a fundamental reason a technique developed for language couldn’t help us understand spatial signals. The question is whether the representation and the learning objective are sufficient.

Language already gives you a very useful abstraction. When you say “a chair,” you’ve compressed away its exact geometry, the lighting, the viewpoint, and many other details. With visual or spatial signals, the model has to discover those abstractions from the observations themselves. And some of the details that language leaves out are precisely what you need to interact with the world—where the chair is, how far away it is, whether you can reach it.

You can turn an image into a sequence of tokens and predict the next token. But making something look like a language-modeling problem doesn’t automatically mean you’ve captured its spatial structure. Two points that are nearby in three-dimensional space might be far apart in your sequence, or one might be hidden from view entirely.

So my concern isn’t really about transformers versus some other architecture. It’s about what we ask the model to learn. Predicting observations can be useful, but we also need to establish whether the model learns geometry, physical relationships, and consistency across viewpoints. Fluent descriptions alone don’t establish that understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says an image can be turned into a token sequence, but it does not state that serializing a global world state produces a highly redundant representation.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify equal attention to every token as a transformer inductive bias.

sol-6.1.text:
I would be careful with the word “cannot.” Language modeling gives us powerful tools, but the question is whether those tools alone give us the right representation of the physical world.

Language is already a highly compressed, discrete description. If I say, “There is a cup on the table,” you know the objects and their relationship, but you don’t know the exact geometry, the depth, or how the appearance changes as you move around. Those details matter if you want a system to interact with that cup.

You can turn an image or a video into tokens and train a model to predict the next token. That can work remarkably well. But tokenizing a spatial signal doesn’t automatically make it equivalent to language. The model still has to learn spatial continuity, geometry, and consistency across viewpoints and over time. A plausible sequence of tokens isn’t necessarily a physically consistent world.

So I don’t think the conclusion should be that transformers or prediction are unsuitable. It’s that we shouldn’t assume the language-modeling recipe, unchanged, solves visual understanding. We need to ask what representations and learning objectives preserve the structure of the world, rather than just produce a convincing description of it.
